# Preface {.unnumbered}

Understanding how organisms react to landscape and habitat structure is a key problem in ecology. It is thus important to know how to quantify and describe landscape patterns. This has motivated the development of hundreds of indices, especially in landscape ecology. Ecologists often used FRAGSTATS to compute such indices using land use or land cover (often abbreviated with LULC) gridded data sets. Unfortunately, FRAGSTATS is not an open source software, and its graphical user interface is not very adapted for reproducible workflows. Fortunately, it is now possible to compute many of these indices with R using the landscapemetrics package.

The first version of this tutorial was created for a course given at the [Swiss Ornithological Institute](https://www.vogelwarte.ch/en){target="_blank"} in 2026. Researchers and students in ecology were the original audience but the whole material can be used by anybody who wants to learn more about how to perform these techniques.

None of this could have been written without the incredible work done by the R-spatial community. I'd especially like to thank all the software developers who created and are maintaining the R software, the R packages and the open-source libraries used in these packages!


# Getting ready {.unnumbered}

You'll need the following packages to run the examples in this book. You can use the following code to install them. All the required dependencies will be automatically installed.

::: callout-important
Please also update to the latest version of R, otherwise you may get packages that are not fully up-to-date.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
packages <- c("terra", "landscapemetrics", "motif")

cat("``` r", paste0('install.packages(','"', packages, '"', ')'), "```", sep = "\n")
```

The required data is available on the GitHub repository (<https://github.com/jguelat/landscape-r>{target="_blank"}). You'll also find all the code needed to re-create the whole book.

# R and packages versions {.unnumbered}

To create this book, the following R version was used:

```{r}
#| eval: false
R.version
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
Rversion <- sapply(R.version, function(x) {x[1]})
Rversion <- data.frame(names(Rversion), Rversion, row.names = NULL)
names(Rversion) <- NULL
#print(Rversion, row.names = FALSE, right = FALSE)
format_tt(tt(Rversion, width = c(1, 2)), quarto = TRUE)
```
\

And the following packages (the dependencies are not listed):

```{r}
#| echo: false
packages <- sort(packages)
versions <- sapply(packages, function(x) {as.character(packageVersion(x))})

packagesData <- data.frame(Package = packages, Version = versions, row.names = NULL)
#print(packagesData, row.names = FALSE, right = FALSE)
format_tt(tt(packagesData, width = c(1, 2)), quarto = TRUE) |> style_tt(i = 1:nrow(packagesData), j = 1, monospace = TRUE)
```
